dd0ee4229a16: <0>1. The "Thirteenth Way Out" (1946).</0> In his Grapevine article "Anonymity" (1946), Bill tells how the book got its title. A narrow vote had favored "The Way Out," but the Library of Congress already had twelve books by that name: "we shivered at the possibility of being the 'Thirteenth Way Out'" (P-17, "Anonymity," 1946). So the book, and the fellowship, became "Alcoholics Anonymous." Bill tells the same story in <1>A.A. Comes of Age</1> (1957). This isn't a step at all. It's a joke about a book title.
3e10fb9bacda: <0>2. Clubs as a "Thirteenth Step" (1947).</0> In "Clubs in A.A." (1947), Bill writes that so many members value clubs that "we might conceive them as a central A.A. institution — a sort of 'Thirteenth Step' of our recovery program without which the other Twelve Steps wouldn't work" (P-17, "Clubs in A.A.," 1947). He raises it as the far end of the pro-club view: some enthusiasts act as if club life alone could handle the drinking problem, and they "are apt to depend upon clubs rather than upon the A.A. program" (P-17, "Clubs in A.A.," 1947). He then gives the opposite view and settles on a middle ground. Members who want clubs should have them, but clubs should be separately incorporated and kept apart from the groups' A.A. affairs, "to separate the material from the spiritual" (P-17, "Clubs in A.A.," 1947). (See <1>What did Bill W. say about clubs and A.A.?</1>)

"Victor" and "Lil" (written 1980, about 1935).</0> <1>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</1> tells of a former Akron mayor and "the first woman to seek help," two of the alcoholics around Akron in the summer and fall of 1935 "who didn't jell" (<2>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</2>, 1980). "Together, Victor and the lady known as Lil started out to write the 'thirteenth step,' long before the first twelve were ever thought of" (<3>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</3>, 1980). It uses it knowingly, for a man and a woman pairing off, and expects the reader to get the joke.

Some of the people once judged hopeless became the group's most respected and best-loved members, and Bill calls those who condemned them "the Pharisees" whose false righteousness did the group "the deeper spiritual damage" (P-17, "Who Is a Member of Alcoholics Anonymous?", 1946).
